articles.title: Cirurgia do 'mais tatuado do Brasil' definirá gravidade de tumor | G1
articles.standfirst: Leandro de Souza descobriu nódulo durante exames de triagem para remover desenhos do rosto. Influenciador ficou conhecido após ter 95% do corpo coberto por mais de 170 tatuagens.
articles.summary: Leandro de Souza descobriu nódulo durante exames de triagem para remover desenhos do rosto. Influenciador ficou conhecido após ter 95% do corpo coberto por mais de 170 tatuagens.
articles.body:
A cirurgia do influenciador Leandro de Souza , conhecido por ter sido considerado o "homem mais tatuado do Brasil" , pode esclarecer os próximos passos do tratamento.

O procedimento chamado Ressecção Transuretral de Tumor (RTU) de bexiga, que deve ser realizado na próxima quarta-feira (16), será determinante para que os médicos avaliem a gravidade do quadro.

➡️ Leandro chegou a ter 95% do corpo coberto por mais de 170 tatuagens, feitas ao longo de duas décadas. A marca foi registrada oficialmente em um evento internacional realizado em Santa Rosa, no Noroeste gaúcho.

Além da retirada do tumor identificado na bexiga , a intervenção permitirá a coleta de material para biópsia, exame que deve indicar se a lesão é benigna ou maligna e definir se serão necessários outros tratamentos após a cirurgia.

A avaliação poderá definir, por exemplo, a adoção de quimioterapia ou radioterapia caso seja constatado câncer.

"Me encaminharam, já autorizaram a minha cirurgia para retirada do tumor, e se Deus quiser, não vai ser preciso mais nada", disse o influenciador após sair da consulta na última quinta-feira (10).

'Homem mais tatuado do Brasil' fará cirurgia para retirar tumor da bexiga — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A descoberta do tumor aconteceu momentos antes da sua sétima sessão de remoção de tatuagens do rosto , em 11 de agosto. Durante a triagem feita pelo biomédico Giancarlo Pincelli, foi descoberto um tumor na bexiga , e o procedimento foi adiado . As sessões são realizadas em uma clínica de Franco da Rocha (SP).

"Comecei a questionar sobre o problema de saúde dele, como é que ele estava. Pensei, eu vou fazer uma ultrassonografia nele. Aí eu liguei para um amigo, médico radiologista, especialista em ultrassonografia", explica Pincelli.

O exame de imagem mostrou o tumor na bexiga. De acordo com ele, o tumor media cerca de 6 centímetros por 5 centímetros .

É descartada qualquer relação entre a remoção das tatuagens e o surgimento do tumor . "Fiz diversas perguntas para o médico e ele falou já não ter nada a ver com o processo de remoção de tatuagem, que já está aqui há muito tempo", diz Pincelli.

Problemas de saúde o fizeram interromper curso

Há cerca de três meses, Leandro foi diagnosticado com insuficiência renal . Ele havia se mudado para Petrolina , em Pernambuco, em fevereiro deste ano, após ganhar uma bolsa de estudos no Seminário Evangélico Betânia (SEB) , para cursar teologia. Ele ficaria por quatro anos na instituição, mas, devido aos problemas de saúde, retornou ao RS no mês de junho, após concluir um semestre de estudos.

O fotógrafo e influenciador digital atua como autônomo e chegou a passar um período em São Paulo nos últimos meses, mas voltou à sua cidade natal para seguir com o tratamento de saúde.

articles.standfirst: Jardim Casqueiro, Ilha Caraguatá, Vila Natal e Vila Nova lideram as remoções, com seis veículos retirados em cada bairro.
articles.summary: Serviço ocorreu em 15 bairros da cidade. Segundo a prefeitura, janeiro foi o mês com mais remoções, com 13 veículos recolhidos.
articles.body:
Cubatão recolhe 45 veículos abandonados das ruas — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura de Cubatão

A Companhia Municipal de Trânsito (CMT) de Cubatão , no litoral de São Paulo, recolheu 45 veículos abandonados em vias públicas. As remoções ocorreram em 15 bairros da cidade.

Segundo a prefeitura, Jardim Casqueiro, Ilha Caraguatá, Vila Natal e Vila Nova concentraram o maior número de recolhimentos, com seis veículos retirados em cada bairro. Na Vila São José, foram cinco.

Na Vila Paulista e no Bolsão 7, três veículos foram recolhidos em cada local. Parque Fernando Jorge e Pinheiro do Miranda tiveram duas remoções cada.

Água Fria, Conjunto Rubens Lara, Jardim Nova República, Parque São Luís, Vila Elizabete e Vila Esperança registraram um veículo recolhido em cada bairro.

Segundo a prefeitura, a ação realizada entre 7 de janeiro e 27 de agosto de 2026 tem como objetivo liberar espaços nas vias públicas, melhorar a circulação e reduzir transtornos provocados por veículos abandonados.

A retirada é feita com base na Lei Municipal nº 3.413/2010. Após a identificação de um veículo abandonado, o proprietário é notificado e tem prazo de 48 horas para retirá-lo do local.

Se o veículo permanecer na via após esse período, ele pode ser guinchado para o pátio da CMT.

articles.title: 'I was stunned': 'Bittu Tabahi' finds dog carcasses, medical waste along Turahalli forest in Bengaluru
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Days after seeking suggestions from his followers on which state he should visit first for a clean-up drive, Madhya Pradesh-based environme.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Days after seeking suggestions from his followers on which state he should visit first for a clean-up drive, Madhya Pradesh-based environment activist Surendra Singh Choudhary, popularly known as Bittu Tabahi, surprised Bengalureans Saturday morning by taking his cleanliness mission beyond his home state for the first time. Known for single-handedly cleaning up a stretch of a river in Madhya Pradesh, Bittu, along with several others, participated in the drive along the periphery of Turahalli forest in Banashankari 6th Stage.Supported by a team of volunteers and local residents, Bittu, along with noted environmentalist AN Yellappa Reddy, and Ramakrishna Ganeshan from India Plog Run, joined the ‘Clean Up Turahalli’ drive organised by The Indian Garage Co in collaboration with Indus Herbs and assisted by Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA).But, Bittu was left stunned by what he encountered along the boundary of the reserve forest. From piles of quintals of poultry waste to domestic sanitary waste and dog carcasses stuffed in duffel bags, medical waste, and heaps of plastic waste were dumped recklessly along the forest periphery. “No matter where you go, we lack civic sense. Keeping our surroundings clean is the least of our priorities. Initially, I thought it would be only plastic waste, but as I started clearing it, I was stunned to find dog carcasses and medical waste underneath the plastic heaps,” Bittu said. The clean-up drive, which began at 8am and lasted nearly four hours, resulted in the removal of over two tonnes of waste.Yellappa Reddy, who launched the drive, said, “The story of Bittu is inspiring, and it is the need of the hour for Gen Z to wake up to the threat of environmental pollution and emulate what Bittu has done back home. Nearly four decades ago, the Turahalli area was a catchment for four mega waterbodies. But today, it is a tragedy that the same environment has become a dumping ground and volunteers have to team up to clean the area. Luckily, due to the hard efforts of forest department, the interiors of the Turahalli reserve forest have remained intact and free from waste infestation.”Bittu remarked, “I thought in Bengaluru, the tech capital of India, the green spaces would be litter-free due to strong civic enforcement. But here, all along the road, there was legacy waste, and our hands alone could not clear the entire thing. A backhoe had to be summoned to clear the waste pile-up. If only trees and forests had bluetooth or Wi-Fi capabilities, people perhaps would not have treated them with such disregard.” He later distributed a variety of saplings to all the volunteers.Bittu, a 21-year-old BSc student, gained worldwide attention after documenting his efforts to clean Ajnar river in Biaora, Rajgarh district of Madhya Pradesh. articles.title: London homes are cracking, sinking: How extreme heat is damaging properties in UK capital
articles.summary: News News: Cracks appearing across walls, doors suddenly refusing to close and windows becoming difficult to open are emerging as a new concern for homeowners in.
articles.body: Cracks appearing across walls, doors suddenly refusing to close and windows becoming difficult to open are emerging as a new concern for homeowners in London after an unusually hot and dry summer. The problem is linked to subsidence, as heat and prolonged dry conditions cause the clay-rich soil beneath homes to shrink and shift.London and parts of southeast England are particularly vulnerable because much of the region is built on clay. When the soil is wet, clay absorbs water and expands. During hot, dry periods, it loses moisture and contracts. If this movement happens unevenly beneath a building, its foundations can shift, causing cracks and other structural problems.The process is known as “shrink-swell”. It becomes particularly significant when the ground beneath different parts of a property moves at different rates.“Subsidence is one of the most damaging geohazards in the UK today,” a spokesperson for the British Geological Survey said, as quoted by CNN.Making the problem worseHigh temperatures are not the only factor. Trees and other vegetation can also contribute to ground movement. During dry conditions, their roots extend deeper into the soil in search of water, drawing moisture from the ground around nearby properties. This can further dry out the clay and cause it to contract.Older homes can be more exposed because they often have shallower foundations. More than half of London's homes were built before 1945, making the city's ageing housing stock an important factor in the risk.The problem is also spreading beyond London and southeast England.“When I started in the business 40 years ago, it was mostly a London and southeast England issue. But with climate change it is now affecting many other parts of the UK as well,” said subsidence expert Bob Gibson, director of Building & Structural Consultants.Every hot, dry summer can trigger a surge in subsidence claims. In 2025, the UK insurance industry paid out a record $415 million in subsidence-related claims, up 10% from the previous year, according to the Association of British Insurers.The pressure has continued this year. Insurers paid more than $97 million in subsidence-related claims in the second quarter of 2026, while the average claim rose to a record $27,000.“Following the extremely hot and dry weather we saw over July and August this year, it’s likely we’ll see more subsidence claims over the coming months,” said Louise Clark, general insurance policy manager at the ABI.What does subsidence mean for homeowners?Subsidence does not necessarily mean a house is about to collapse. But it can cause serious and expensive damage, including cracks in walls, distorted door and window frames and problems with foundations.The extent of the damage depends on both the underlying ground conditions and how vulnerable the building is.“There are two ingredients to consider in subsidence risk,” said Brunella Balzano, senior lecturer in structural design at Cardiff University. “The vulnerability of the building and the hazard itself.”Homeowners may have limited options for addressing the underlying ground movement. Measures can include removing trees or vegetation close to the property, installing barriers to prevent roots from reaching the foundations and, in more severe cases, underpinning the building by strengthening or extending its foundations.But the growing risk is also creating a problem for the property insurance market.“I think it’s possible … that in the near future, subsidence might not be insured anymore,” Balzano said.Homeowners in high-risk areas are already reporting difficulties obtaining cover. Gibson said insurers were “jacking-up premiums hugely, or not inviting renewal of subsidence cover”.That creates another property-market concern: serious subsidence can reduce a home's value, make it harder to sell and leave owners facing substantial repair costs.London's particular vulnerability comes from the type of clay beneath much of the city. Some of these soils contain expansive minerals that respond strongly to changes in moisture.That means a combination of prolonged heat, drought and vegetation can produce ground movement beneath buildings.The risk is expected to increase as temperatures rise. British Geological Survey data indicates that more than 26% of properties in London could be affected by subsidence by 2070 if global warming continues at roughly its current pace.For homeowners, the warning signs can therefore be more than cosmetic. New or widening cracks, sticking doors and distorted windows can indicate movement in the building and may warrant a professional assessment.Subsidence is generally a gradual process rather than an immediate threat to life. But as extreme heat and drought become more frequent, ground movement is becoming an increasingly important consideration for Britain's housing stock, insurance costs and property values.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Iran, Oman agree on details of new entry and exit routes for Strait of Hormuz, says report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran and Oman have agreed on details of new entry and exit routes for the Strait of Hormuz and will brief Gulf countries on the outcome of their consu.
articles.body: Iran and Oman have agreed on details of new entry and exit routes for the Strait of Hormuz and will brief Gulf countries on the outcome of their consultations at a regional meeting in Muscat on Monday, Iranian officials said on Saturday.The development comes amid heightened tensions in West Asia, with the strategic waterway remaining a key focus of regional and international attention.Citing a source close to Iran’s negotiating team, semi-official Tasnim news agency said the understanding was reached after “intensive technical and diplomatic talks between Iran and Oman, which culminated in a final agreement in late August.”Under the proposed arrangement, the entry route from the Gulf “lies entirely within Iran's territorial waters”, while part of the exit route also falls “within Iranian territorial waters”, Tasnim news said quoting sources.The source added that the routes would operate under Iranian arrangements and that the southern route would be closed once the new system becomes operational. The United States had insisted that the southern route be opened, the source said.“The understanding in no way means that the Strait of Hormuz will be opened,” the source said, adding that Iran had seven conditions for reopening the waterway and had conveyed them to the United States.The source said the strait would remain closed unless those conditions were implemented, with any reopening depending entirely on US actions.Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Friday that foreign ministers of Gulf littoral states would meet in Oman on Monday to discuss regional issues, including the Iran-Oman consultations on designating safe routes through the Strait of Hormuz.Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Baghaei said the meeting would “hopefully” include foreign ministers from Gulf countries, Iran and Iraq.“As part of the agenda, we are going to brief the delegations about the results of the Iran and Oman consultations regarding the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that the consultations were held by Iran and Oman as “the two coastal states of the Strait of Hormuz.”Late last month, Iran and Oman said in a joint statement that they had exchanged views on a proposed phased framework that included establishing a temporary joint shipping corridor in the strait.According to the Bahrain News Agency, Bahrain’s foreign ministry said it would not participate in any collective meeting involving Iran until diplomatic relations between the two countries are restored.Bahrain severed diplomatic ties with Iran in January 2016. The ministry said it had conveyed its position to Oman through official channels, while stressing that this did not diminish its appreciation of Oman’s efforts or its commitment to dialogue.It said dialogue could not be based on ignoring facts, pointing to attacks on Bahrain’s infrastructure and civilian sites. The ministry also said the reported targeting of Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline showed that civilian and economic facilities remained under threat.The Strait of Hormuz connects the Gulf with the Arabian Sea and is one of the world’s most important routes for oil and gas shipments. Iran and Oman sit on opposite sides of the waterway and have continued consultations on maritime security and navigation.Following US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, Tehran restricted passage through the strait, while US forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels travelling to and from Iranian ports.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A former fuel-tank farm beside an Alaska national park visitor center has been erased; a young conservation crew restored 15,000 square yards of landscape and built 500 feet of new trail
articles.summary: US News: What was once a utilitarian patch of ground beside an Alaska visitor center is now becoming part of the landscape again. At Lake Clark National Park a.
articles.body: What was once a utilitarian patch of ground beside an Alaska visitor center is now becoming part of the landscape again. At Lake Clark National Park and Preserve, a young conservation crew has spent the summer replacing an old fuel-tank farm with trails, vegetation and safer spaces for visitors. According to the latest news release by National Park Service, the project at Port Alsworth comes as more people are discovering the remote national park. By August 2026, visitation was already 43% higher than during the entire 2024 season, the last year the park operated fully.From fuel storage to public spaceThe restoration focused on roughly 15,000 square yards beside the Port Alsworth Visitor Center, states the news release. The area had previously been occupied by fuel tanks, leaving a landscape that was hardly suited to the growing number of visitors arriving at the park. Over 10 weeks, a Maintenance Action Team crew from the Student Conservation Association transformed the site. According to the report, one of the biggest changes was the construction of a new parking area, helping improve the flow of vehicles around the visitor center. The former tank farm was also revegetated, allowing the disturbed ground to begin blending back into its surroundings.The work was designed with more than appearance in mind. Better pedestrian routes and vehicle access are expected to make the area safer as visitor numbers continue to rise.A new link into the parkThe project also created about 500 feet of new pedestrian trail, connecting the visitor center with the Lakeview Tinitun trail and the broader trail network. That connection gives visitors a clearer route toward some of Lake Clark's best-known hiking destinations, including the Tanalian Mountain and Tanalian Falls trails. The crew also maintained four miles of existing trails, ensuring that improvements extended beyond the immediate visitor-center area.Young workers learn the tradesThe restoration was carried out by a young adult Maintenance Action Team, a program that gives participants practical experience in traditional construction and maintenance skills, states the report. Working alongside National Park Service employees, crew members gained experience that ranged from trail maintenance to site construction and landscape restoration. The program serves a dual purpose: helping national parks complete demanding projects while introducing younger workers to trades that are increasingly important to the preservation of historic and natural places. For Lake Clark, that combination was particularly valuable. The project delivered immediate improvements to a heavily used visitor area while giving a new generation hands-on experience in maintaining public lands.Preparing for a busier futureFor the uninitiated, Lake Clark is one of Alaska's more remote national parks, but its growing popularity is creating new demands on its infrastructure. The Port Alsworth restoration offers a practical response. An area once dedicated to fuel storage has been converted into a more welcoming gateway, with new vegetation, parking and trails guiding visitors naturally toward the park's wider landscape. The transformation may not be the kind of dramatic change that dominates photographs of Alaska. Instead, its success lies in making the visitor experience feel more natural, safer and easier to navigate. For a national park facing a surge in visitors, that quiet improvement could prove just as important as the wilderness beyond the trailhead.Image Courtesy: National Park ServiceCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the "growing strength, appeal and unprecedented trust" in Brics during the second day of the multilateral event in New Delhi.While chairing the Brics session on "Inclusive global governance and strengthening multilateralism", PM Modi said that cooperation and support between the Brics members has led the shared vision transform in a "win-win cooperation."We warmly welcome you all to the extended family of Brics. Today, this auditorium is bringing together different continents, cultures and development journeys. This is a testament to the growing strength, appeal and unprecedented trust in Brics," PM Modi said."Under India's Brics presidency, we have focused all our efforts on four pillars: resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. I am pleased that with your cooperation and support, we have been able to transform our shared vision into a win-win cooperation," he added.The Prime Minister also said that the number of tensions in the world is continuously increasing and no crisis remains confined to one region."Today, the number of tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and they are having a very negative and widespread impact on the lives of ordinary people. Pandemics, climate disasters and supply chain disruptions have shown that in today's interconnected world, no crisis remains confined to one region," PM Modi said."Therefore, we have placed special emphasis on strengthening resilience within the Brics group. It is equally important to identify challenges in time, prepare for them and take immediate action. With this approach, an integrated Brics early warning system has been agreed upon for the prevention of and response to infectious diseases. For disaster management, early warning data integration guidelines have been prepared. The BRICS Logistics Supply Chain Cooperation Framework will help make our supply chains more reliable and resilient," he added.Earlier, PM Modi, along with world leaders, posed for a family photo of the Brics grouping at Bharat Mandapam.PM Modi stood in the centre with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping beside him.The last leg of the summit is focused on the core pillars of India's 2026 Brics chairship -- resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. articles.title: In 2017, a Washington couple began building homeless shelters that assembled in under an hour; after reportedly sheltering more than 30,000 people, their company is shutting down
articles.summary: US News: Pallet, a company that revolutionized emergency homelessness solutions by providing rapidly assembled shelters, is shutting down after helping over 30,000 people in nine years. Explore the impact and future of temporary shelter solutions as they prepare to cease operations.
articles.body: In 2017, a husband-and-wife team in Washington began experimenting with a different way to provide emergency shelter. Rather than constructing conventional buildings that could take weeks or months, Amy and Brady King wanted to create small, durable units that could be transported easily and assembled rapidly. Their idea eventually became Pallet, an Everett-based company that built villages of temporary shelters for people experiencing homelessness.According to GeekWire, Pallet is closing its business after nine years of building transitional shelters for people experiencing homelessness. The company reported that its villages across the United States and Canada had offered more than 6,083 beds and sheltered an estimated 30,000 people. Its closure ends a company that made rapid construction central to its approach to homelessness. The shelters could be assembled in under an hour, but the larger challenge was creating places where people could live indoors, access support services and begin working toward permanent housing.A shelter designed to go up quicklyThe Kings had construction experience before starting Pallet and initially considered using their modular shelters for people displaced by natural disasters. The design consisted of durable panels that could be transported flat and assembled on site with minimal tools. Their first major opportunity came from the homelessness crisis closer to home. According to the City of Tacoma, the city had declared a state of emergency over homelessness in 2017 and began using micro-shelters as part of its emergency response.Pallet became an early supplier, with Tacoma eventually incorporating 40 of its shelters into a sanctioned tent city. The small units were designed as temporary accommodation, with communal facilities provided elsewhere in the village. Pallet’s prefabricated modules could be installed on site and assembled in about an hour without specialised tools. The units had basic amenities, including a folding bed, windows, ventilation, and locking doors and offered residents a private place, while other communal services could be placed somewhere else in the village. These structures could be installed far faster than conventional buildings, making them useful for communities that needed rapid shelter.From emergency shelter to a transitional villagePallet's concept was not intended to replace permanent housing. Instead, its shelters were designed as transitional spaces where residents could move indoors while receiving support from service providers. That distinction shaped the way the villages operated. The shelter itself provided a private sleeping space, while kitchens, bathrooms, laundry facilities and other services could be shared throughout the wider site. Case managers and partner organisations could work with residents on issues such as employment, benefits, healthcare and finding permanent accommodation. A review published in Wellbeing, Space and Society in 2026 examined research on tiny homes and sleeping cabins in high-income countries and found that these approaches could form part of a broader response to homelessness, while also noting that evidence on their effectiveness remains limited.Pallet nevertheless expanded rapidly. The company eventually built its 100th village and supplied shelters to communities across North America. Its workforce model was also part of the company's mission. Pallet said it employed people with lived experience of homelessness and other barriers to conventional employment, linking shelter production with a so-called fair-chance employment approach. The model combined rapid construction with communal services and a path toward more stable housing.Nine years, 30,000 people and an unexpected endingHowever, Pallet later faced sustainability challenges as conditions around homelessness changed. In its shutdown announcement in September 2026, the company said customer demands had become more complex and that funding conditions and political priorities were shifting.The decision came despite the company’s scale. Pallet says its villages across the US and Canada had provided more than 6,083 beds and sheltered over 30,000 people since 2017. Its shelters also helped popularise a rapid-deployment housing model that some communities continued to use. The closure also raises questions about what will happen to the infrastructure now that the company is gone. According to Pallet, operators of existing villages will be able to access warranty information and replacement parts, but maintenance will be their responsibility.Pallet’s closure is an ironic ending for a company built around rapid shelter deployment. The company showed how quickly emergency shelter could be manufactured, transported and assembled for thousands of people. But fast assembly alone could not address housing affordability, government support or homelessness itself. The shelters were meant to last for years, but the company that produced them lasted only nine years.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2019, Britain laid tyre-rubber asphalt on the M1; after successful trials, it won UK industry approval in 2021, with up to 750 waste tyres reusable per kilometre
articles.summary: UK News: Britain began testing an unusual solution to its mounting tyre waste in 2019, when Highways England and construction company Tarmac laid a road surfac.
articles.body: Britain began testing an unusual solution to its mounting tyre waste in 2019, when Highways England and construction company Tarmac laid a road surface containing recycled tyre rubber on the M1 near Leicester, according to a UK government press release published that August. The trial tested whether granulated rubber from waste tyres could be incorporated into asphalt durable enough for a heavily trafficked motorway. Two years later, Tarmac said the material had secured BBA HAPAS Clause 942 approval for use on the UK’s strategic road network, marking a significant step towards its wider adoption.From waste tyres to motorway surfaceThe original trial was carried out on the southbound M1 between junctions 23 and 22. Tarmac developed the asphalt by incorporating granulated rubber recovered from end-of-life tyres into the road mix.The experiment was designed to test whether the material could withstand the demands of one of Britain’s busiest road networks while also tackling a growing waste problem. At the time, Highways England said around 40 million waste tyres were generated in the UK each year. The 2019 trial was intended to assess whether using some of that material in roads could provide an alternative to exporting or otherwise disposing of used tyres. Rather than simply replacing conventional asphalt with whole tyres, the process uses processed tyre rubber as a component of the asphalt mixture.How many tyres can one kilometre use?Tarmac estimates that the rubber recovered from up to 750 waste tyres can be incorporated into each kilometre of highway, depending on the thickness of the road surface. Its current product information describes the material as a warm-mix asphalt containing recycled rubber crumb from end-of-life car tyres.That figure is an estimate rather than a fixed number for every road. The amount of rubber that can be incorporated depends on the design and thickness of the particular surface. The approach also gives old tyres another use within the UK rather than sending them overseas. Tarmac said in 2021 that the country was still exporting a significant share of its used tyres, making road construction an additional domestic route for tyre recycling.From M1 trial to industry approvalThe M1 experiment was not an isolated test. Tarmac said its rubber-modified asphalt had undergone a series of trials before the company announced in April 2021 that its ULTIPAVE R system had received BBA HAPAS Clause 942 approval.The approval is significant because Clause 942 covers thin surfacing systems used on roads, including the strategic road network. Tarmac described ULTIPAVE R as the first thin surfacing system of its kind in the UK to receive that approval.The British Board of Agrément’s certification record confirms that ULTIPAVE-R is a stone mastic asphalt incorporating ground tyre rubber and is assessed for use as a warm-mix surface course in new and maintenance road construction. The current certificate records the product as originally certified in August 2020.More than just recyclingThe rubber is only one part of the sustainability pitch. Tarmac’s ULTIPAVE R uses its ULTILOW warm-mix technology, which allows the asphalt to be produced at lower temperatures than conventional hot-mix asphalt. The company says this reduces embodied carbon during production.The idea also fits into a broader push to make road construction more circular, instead of treating used tyres solely as a disposal problem, part of their material can be recovered and incorporated into new infrastructure.The M1 trial therefore represented more than an experiment in changing what roads are made from. It tested whether one of Britain’s largest waste streams could be given a second life beneath the wheels of the vehicles generating the demand for new roads in the first place.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Priced out of Melbourne, an Australian couple bought 1.5 hectares in Tasmania for $330,000; in 2022 they began a recycled bottle Earthship and completed the home nearly three years later for $880,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For Matt Ellis and Kate Tucker, buying a home in Melbourne became a familiar cycle of hope, bidding and disappointment. The couple wanted to remain cl.
articles.body: For Matt Ellis and Kate Tucker, buying a home in Melbourne became a familiar cycle of hope, bidding and disappointment. The couple wanted to remain close to their community and friends, but they were repeatedly outbid in the inner city market. Eventually, they looked far beyond Victoria and found a more affordable path near Cygnet in Tasmania. They bought 1.5 hectares of land for $330,000 in early 2019 and started planning an unusual home based on the Earthship movement. They began building in 2022 using recycled bottles, rammed earth and passive solar principles. Nearly three years later, their home was finished at a total cost of $880,000. As reported by ABC News, the project became a demanding family build supported by volunteers, workshops and a shared belief that a sustainable home could also be modern, comfortable and personal.Leaving Melbourne behindMatt and Kate had long imagined living in the countryside, but their first preference was to find a home in or near Melbourne. They wanted to stay connected to friends and the community they knew. The problem was the property market. Again and again, the couple found themselves competing against buyers with deeper pockets.For many families, being priced out of a city means making a difficult choice between location, space and affordability. Matt and Kate eventually decided that land offered more possibilities than a finished house. Rather than stretching their finances to buy a conventional property, they looked for somewhere they could build a home around their values.The answer came in Tasmania, just outside the town of Cygnet, about 40 minutes from Hobart. The 1.5 hectare property provided room for a home, gardens, a greenhouse and another planned residence for Matt’s father. At $330,000, the land cost far less than the properties they had been unable to secure in Melbourne.The move was not simply an escape from high prices. It gave the couple an opportunity to pursue a long held dream of designing an Earthship.What an Earthship isEarthships are homes designed to work with natural systems rather than rely entirely on conventional utilities. The movement began in New Mexico during the 1970s under architect Michael Reynolds. Earthship designs often use recycled materials, passive solar heating, water collection, food growing and systems for treating household waste.The approach is based on reducing dependence on external power, water and sewage networks. Thick walls help regulate indoor temperatures, while windows are positioned to capture winter sunlight and limit overheating. Greenhouses can provide food growing space and help warm the home.The concept has attracted people interested in sustainability, resilience and lower long term running costs. It has also remained relatively uncommon in Australia. According to the couple’s building designer, Martin Freney, only about 15 Earthships had been completed across the country at the time of the project.Traditional Earthships are often associated with curved forms, earth packed tyres and unusual, almost futuristic appearances. Matt and Kate wanted to use the principles without copying the look. Their home would have sharper lines and a contemporary appearance, while retaining the core ideas of passive heating, recycled materials and self sufficiency.Designing for TasmaniaThe couple’s design had to respond to Tasmania’s cooler climate. Earthship homes in New Mexico are built for a very different environment, with intense sun, hot days and cold nights. A direct copy would not have worked well on a Tasmanian site.Instead of using the traditional earth floor, the Cygnet home has a concrete foundation to avoid the chill associated with a ground level floor in a cool climate. The design also includes tubes within the foundation that transfer heat from the ground, helping maintain a more stable indoor temperature.The walls were planned as monolithic rammed earth structures. These walls act as thermal mass, absorbing warmth during the day and releasing it slowly as temperatures fall. The method reduces the need for conventional heating and cooling, although it does not eliminate the need for careful design and maintenance.North facing windows were positioned to make the most of available sunlight. Inside, the greenhouse became a defining feature, bringing natural light into the home and providing a space for growing plants. The greenhouse also creates a transition between the outside environment and the living areas.Recycled bottles become building materialsOne of the most recognisable features of the home is its use of recycled bottle bricks. Rather than sending empty bottles to landfill or relying entirely on new construction materials, the bottles were incorporated into sections of the building.Bottle bricks allow light to filter through walls and create colourful visual details. They also express the Earthship philosophy of turning waste into a resource. For the family, the bottles became part of the home’s identity, connecting the building to the wider community effort that helped construct it.Using recycled materials does not automatically make a building inexpensive. Materials must be collected, cleaned, prepared and installed safely. You may also need specialist advice and careful approval from local authorities for unusual methods of construction. Matt and Kate’s experience showed that sustainable materials can reduce waste and add character, but they still demand time, labour and planning.When the build fell behindThe original plan was ambitious. The couple expected both Earthship homes to take about 15 months to build, with a projected cost of roughly $600,000 per house. They believed the price would be comparable to a conventional custom home, but that the finished result would offer greater energy efficiency and lower operating costs.The project encountered problems almost immediately. The carpenter leading the construction became seriously ill, creating a major disruption. Weeks of rain slowed progress further. Timelines stretched, costs rose and the couple faced the pressure of continuing full time work while raising young children.Their lease on a nearby rental home was also running out, adding urgency to an already difficult project. The family needed a way to make the house liveable while construction continued.Instead of relying only on contractors, Matt and Kate turned to the wider Earthship community.Strangers help build a homeThe couple had previously attended Earthship workshops, where participants learned construction techniques while helping build experimental or private homes. They decided to host a similar event at their own property.Volunteers arrived for a week long workshop, bringing labour, enthusiasm and practical skills. They learned how to work with cob, make bricks and contribute to the construction. The couple provided food and accommodation, while participants gained experience with an unusual building method.The volunteer effort did more than speed up construction. It helped restore the family’s motivation at a time when the project felt overwhelming. Building a home can be isolating when delays and financial pressure accumulate. Working alongside people who believed in the same ideas gave Matt and Kate a renewed sense of purpose.Some volunteers even stayed overnight in the unfinished house before Matt and Kate moved in. The project became a community experience, and at least one person who attended the workshop later began an Earthship project of their own.The final cost and completionThe couple’s first home took nearly three years to complete and cost $880,000, substantially more than the original estimate. Construction finished in July 2025.The final home is sleek and contemporary rather than rustic or cave like. Earth toned interiors soften the sharp architectural lines, while north facing windows bring sunlight into the living areas. The greenhouse is bright, peaceful and central to the family’s daily life.The home’s sustainable features include rammed earth walls, recycled bottle bricks, passive solar design and systems intended to reduce reliance on conventional heating and cooling. These features are part of a wider design rather than isolated decorations.Matt and Kate have said they do not regret leaving Melbourne or pursuing the project, despite the higher than expected cost and the stress of the build. The home represents more than an alternative construction method. It reflects the life they hoped to create when conventional housing became unaffordable.Work has continued on the second home planned for Matt’s father, with completion estimated for March 2026.A home that teaches its own lessonsThe Cygnet Earthship shows that sustainable housing is not necessarily a shortcut to cheap housing. Recycled materials may reduce waste, but construction can still be expensive. Specialist design, planning requirements, delays and labour all affect the final price.What the project does provide is a different form of value. Passive heating may reduce energy demand. Water and waste systems can offer greater independence from utilities. Recycled materials can give a home a distinct identity while diverting waste from landfill. A greenhouse can provide food, light and a calm place for family members to gather.The process also demonstrates the importance of community. Matt and Kate’s home was not built entirely by the couple or by a single contractor. It developed through the knowledge of designers, the work of volunteers and the encouragement of people who shared their interest in Earthship construction.Their story makes the design feel less like an abstract architectural concept and more like a lived experience. It involved fear, financial pressure, illness, rain and exhaustion, but also friendship, learning and persistence.Choosing a different definition of successFor Matt and Kate, success was not simply building the cheapest possible house. It was creating a home that aligned with their values and gave their family space to live differently.Their experience also reflects a growing interest in alternatives to conventional housing. Rising property prices have encouraged many people to consider smaller towns, regional land, owner building and unconventional materials. Not every project will suit every family, and building outside standard methods can involve significant risks. But the demand for homes that are affordable, efficient and environmentally responsible continues to grow.The Cygnet Earthship offers one possible response. It does not present a perfect formula, and its final cost was much higher than first expected. Yet it shows how people can combine technology, natural systems and community labour to create a home with a strong sense of place.When their son observed that hardly anyone else had a house like theirs, he captured the project’s most personal achievement. The building is unusual, but it is also recognisably theirs, shaped by their choices, their struggles and the people who helped bring it to life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: IDF warns of rising West Bank tensions despite low terror levels, pushes for preventive operations
articles.summary: Security officials say terror activity in the West Bank is at its lowest level since 2011, but warn of growing friction, weapons concerns and potential escal...
articles.body:
Terror activity in the West Bank is at its lowest level since 2011, but security officials warn of potential escalation and growing friction ahead of the holidays.

Hamas headquarters in various locations are likely to attempt terror plots targeting Israelis and IDF soldiers despite the low level of terror activity attributed to combined operations by security forces.

Security officials are concerned about increased friction on the ground due to the growth of new communities, lone farms, and illegal outposts in the West Bank, prompting the IDF to rethink its security approach.

Security officials say terror activity in the West Bank is at its lowest level since 2011, but warn of growing friction, weapons concerns and potential escalation ahead of the holidays.

Despite the fact that terror levels in the West Bank are very low, the lowest since 2011, security officials warned on Sunday that Hamas headquarters in Turkey, Gaza, Iran, Qatar, Lebanon, and other locations will likely attempt to advance terror plots targeting Israelis and IDF soldiers.

The low level of terror activity is attributed to combined operations by the Judea and Samaria Division , commanded by Brig.-Gen. Kobi Heller, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police and Border Police.

Ahead of the holidays, the Judea and Samaria Division carried out extensive preventive operations, targeting not only suspects involved in terror activity but also incitement hubs, in an effort to minimize the potential for attacks in the area.

IDF expands preventive operations amid rising friction

According to security officials, "the IDF enjoys broad freedom of action in Judea and Samaria, especially after it captured the refugee camps in the West Bank, established a presence there, and built supporting infrastructure for rapid activity. In addition, outposts are being built that will strengthen the hold."

Another development security officials view positively is the extensive scope of terror-prevention operations carried out on the ground and in the air . According to IDF data, five terrorists were eliminated by Israeli forces in various incidents over the past week.

However, a source of concern is a new trend of increased friction on the ground. Security officials said the trend is growing, partly due to the significant increase in the number of new communities, with 84 added to the 180 existing communities in the West Bank, as well as the growth in the number of lone farms, which stands at around 140, and illegal outposts, of which there are more than 100.

This security reality requires the IDF to rethink its approach and update its security concept regarding communities and farms that have received state approval, so that they are not left at a disadvantage or facing a gap compared with hostile elements in the area.

Security officials warn of potential escalation scenarios

At the same time, the security establishment emphasizes that security coordination with the Palestinian security services has been maintained, alongside exceptional incidents that require constant monitoring and alertness. In addition, there is a large quantity of weapons held by the Palestinian Authority, alongside weapons smuggling across the Israel-Jordan border.

One extreme scenario being examined is the "turning of the guns" scenario, in which the Palestinian Authority enters a succession struggle over Mahmoud Abbas's position and, during clashes, weapons are turned against IDF soldiers and Israeli civilians. The political leadership has instructed officials to increase preparedness for such a possibility.

According to security sources, Defense Minister Israel Katz may pressure the IDF to capture additional refugee camps and carry out broader operations, with an emphasis on the West Bank, in order to reduce terror activity.

articles.title: Japan's Ocean Postbox: In 1999, a Japanese postmaster sank a working mailbox 33 feet into Susami Bay to attract visitors; by 2018, divers had mailed nearly 38,000 waterproof letters
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover Japan's extraordinary underwater postbox in Susami Bay, where nearly 38,000 waterproof postcards have been mailed since its inception in 1999. A unique tourist attraction and Guinness World Record holder, this mailbox transforms a small fishing town into a diving hotspot.
articles.body: Susami, a small fishing town on the Kii Peninsula in Japan's Wakayama Prefecture, struggled towards the end of the 1990s to offer tourists a reason to stay rather than just pass by on their route to somewhere larger. With only a few thousand residents and no notable landmark to divert tourists from the major coastal route, local authorities were searching for anything unique enough to place the town on a map that largely disregarded it. The man in charge of the neighbourhood post office gave a somewhat surprising answer. As part of a local fair intended to promote the neighbouring Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trail, Toshihiko Matsumoto, who had worked for Japan's postal office for around forty years, suggested erecting a functional mailbox on the floor of Susami Bay. The community dropped a red postbox to a depth of around ten metres, or thirty-three feet, in 1999 with the assistance of a local dive shop, and connected it to the postal system as an officially recognised collecting site.How the underwater postbox worksDivers first buy a waterproof postcard and write their message on dry land with an oil-based paint marker before entering the water. They carry the completed card down to the postbox and place it inside the cast-iron box, which is designed to keep the mail from drifting away while remaining open to the surrounding water.The town rotates two boxes since the metal box rusts steadily in seawater. Every few months, the one in use is replaced so the other may be repaired and painted before it collapses again. Nearly every day, a dive shop employee goes down to the box, picks up whatever has gathered, and, just like any other piece of mail, carries the postcards to the Susami post office for the last leg of their journey. Record keepers were persuaded to take the underwater box seriously in part because it actually feeds into the regular postal network rather than existing only as a curiosity.Earning a place in the record booksBy the early 2000s, word of the unusual mailbox had spread widely enough among divers that the site was formally recognised by Guinness World Records as the deepest underwater postbox in the world, a title which said that in the first year of the box's life, almost four thousand pieces of undersea mail had been collected. The record helped transform a small fishing hamlet into an unusual stop for scuba divers who go to the Kii Peninsula just to mail a postcard from the ocean below.Divers who make the trip often describe the experience as oddly touching, less because of the postcard itself than because of the weird thrill of seeing an utterly quotidian act of communication take place in a place where it was obviously never meant to be. Almost two decades after Matsumoto initially proposed the idea, the numbers interested in the project had risen well beyond what anyone at that original fair could have expected.Twenty years of mail under the seaA documentary produced in 2018 recorded that nearly thirty-eight thousand waterproof postcards had been mailed from the Susami postbox since it first went into the water, a milestone achieved almost solely through word of mouth among divers rather than any continuous advertising push. Matsumoto didn't live to see the project become so famous, but the dive shop owners who inherited the care of the box still talk about the idea as the one thing that made Susami so well known. What started as a rather modest gesture, a postmaster’s idea of livening up a local fair, has outlived the fair itself by more than two decades, proof that sometimes the tiniest ideas at a town festival are the ones that go the farthest.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ukraine deploys drone specialists to Africa, Middle East to target Russian interests: Report
articles.summary: Europe News: Ukraine has expanded its fight against Russia beyond the battlefield at home, deploying drone specialists to Africa and military teams to the Middle E.
articles.body: Ukraine has expanded its fight against Russia beyond the battlefield at home, deploying drone specialists to Africa and military teams to the Middle East to train forces fighting Russian- and Iranian-made drones, according to a CNN report.CNN, citing Ukrainian soldiers, officers and a Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source, reported that around 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed in northern Mali, where they were helping Tuareg-led rebel forces fighting Russian troops and providing drone training, operational support and tactical assistance.The deployments were part of Kyiv’s effort to target Russian interests wherever Moscow has established a military presence, the report said. Ukrainian officials have previously acknowledged providing information to the Tuareg rebels, although Kyiv later denied substantial cooperation with them.One Ukrainian drone operator in Mali told CNN that he coordinated missions remotely, receiving drone signals over the internet and directing rebel fighters by radio. The Ukrainian team was not directly involved in frontline combat, according to the report.Beyond the battlefieldThe deployment comes as Russia has deepened its military presence across Africa, particularly in the Sahel. Moscow initially relied on the Wagner Group but later incorporated its remaining forces into the Africa Corps following the death of Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023.The Ukrainian team in Mali is working with the Azawad Liberation Front, a separatist movement largely made up of northern Tuareg rebels. Ukrainian specialists also helped train the rebels and assisted them during their takeover of the strategic northern city of Kidal earlier this year.The Russian defence ministry accused Kyiv of playing a role in the Kidal assault, alleging that Ukrainian and European instructors had trained the rebels. Ukraine has denied substantial involvement.Ukraine’s overseas military cooperation extends beyond Africa. Ukrainian military experts were sent to at least five Middle Eastern countries after Iran began attacking US allies earlier this year. The teams trained local forces to counter Iranian-made Shahed drones, which Russia has extensively used against Ukraine.In return for the training, Kyiv secured security cooperation agreements and promises of ammunition, the report said.Ukraine has also deployed naval drone operators to northwestern Libya, where Ukrainian Defense Intelligence personnel have been stationed since late 2025, according to a Ukrainian intelligence source cited by CNN. One operator told the outlet that his unit used a military base in Misrata to target Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers while training local forces.The existence of Ukrainian personnel in Libya was first reported by French public broadcaster RFI and has not been officially confirmed by Kyiv.The overseas missions are also giving Ukrainian forces an opportunity to adapt their drone expertise to very different battlefields. A Ukrainian operator told CNN that Mali’s extreme heat, dust and vast terrain created different challenges from the high-intensity warfare in Ukraine.“In Ukraine, it’s high intensity, massive strikes, constant pressure,” the operator said. “Here it’s more of a maneuverable war over large territories, ambushes, route control, working in small groups and depending on knowledge of the terrain.”Drone diplomacy and its risksHéni Nsaibia, West Africa senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, told CNN that Russia had become crucial to the Malian regime, with Africa Corps forces helping prevent a deeper collapse of the government.The first allegations of Ukrainian assistance to the Tuaregs emerged in 2024 after rebels ambushed Wagner and Malian forces near Tinzaouaten. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence spokesperson Andriy Yusov said at the time that the rebels had received “necessary information” to fight Russian forces.Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso subsequently accused Ukraine of sponsoring terrorism in a complaint to the UN Security Council.Russia has also accused Ukraine of involvement in massacres of civilians in Mali, allegations Kyiv has denied. Human Rights Watch has separately accused Russian forces in Mali of killing civilians and said all parties involved in an April escalation unlawfully attacked civilians.The overseas operations reflect Kyiv’s growing attempt to use its battlefield experience as a foreign-policy tool. A Ukrainian Defense Intelligence source told CNN that the aim was to pressure Russia and undermine Moscow’s position as a reliable security partner.Ukraine’s expanding footprint has not been without risks. Earlier this year, a Ukrainian naval drone carrying explosives escaped from operators in Libya and was later found floating near Greece’s Lefkada island. Greece lodged a diplomatic protest, while Kyiv apologised and blamed Russia’s use of a “shadow” fleet for creating the circumstances that led to the incident.Ukraine has long participated in UN peacekeeping missions in Africa, but its current deployments represent a more direct effort to challenge Russian military influence on the continent.Kyrylo Budanov, Ukraine’s former intelligence chief and now head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office, said in 2023 that Ukraine would seek to target Russian interests “anywhere on the face of this world” until it achieved victory.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2006, NBA star Yao Ming publicly rejected shark-fin soup; WildAid later reported consumption across mainland China had fallen by 80% since 2011
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how NBA star Yao Ming's rejection of shark fin soup led to a significant decline in consumption across China by over 80%. Explore the impact of celebrity activism and government intervention on shark conservation efforts.
articles.body: In 2006, one of China’s most recognisable sporting stars helped bring a conservation message to millions of people. Yao Ming, then an NBA star with the Houston Rockets, publicly pledged to stop eating shark-fin soup after learning about shark finning and the pressure demand for the dish placed on shark populations. His decision became part of a wider WildAid campaign that tried to change not just government policy, but the social appeal of a dish traditionally associated with wealth, weddings and formal banquets.At the time, the scale of the trade made the challenge enormous. Shark-fin soup had long been associated with wealth, prestige and formal banquets in China, while the country had become a major market for shark fins. According to WildAid's 2007 shark consumption survey, its study with the China Wildlife Conservation Association, conducted between October 2005 and January 2006 across 16 major Chinese cities, found that 80 per cent of interviewees did not know what shark fin was made from. The survey also found that 35 per cent of those interviewed had consumed shark fin, highlighting the gap between the popularity of the dish and public understanding of its connection to sharks.When a celebrity changed the conversationYao’s significance came from more than celebrity alone. He was a sports celebrity in China and the United States because of his career. By associating his name with shark conservation, WildAid could bring an environmental message into mainstream advertising. The campaign's message was deliberately simple: consumers could influence what happened to sharks by refusing to buy the product. Yao appeared in public-service advertisements in which he rejected shark-fin soup and urged viewers to consider what happened to the animals behind the dish. Other celebrities, including Jackie Chan and later Sir Richard Branson, joined related WildAid campaigns.Research published in Environmental Communication has examined Yao's role in these campaigns and cautioned against assuming that celebrity advertising alone caused the decline in consumption. The research points to other important factors, including Chinese government austerity measures and restrictions on shark fin at official banquets. That distinction matters because the decline was the result of several forces operating at the same time. Yet the campaigns clearly helped change awareness. WildAid reported that in 2008, 55 per cent of surveyed people in Beijing remembered its shark-fin campaign, while 82 per cent of those respondents said they would reduce or stop their consumption as a result. By 2009, the organisation reported that awareness of the problems associated with shark-fin consumption had risen substantially.From luxury dish to declining demandThe next major shift came through government intervention. In 2012, shark-fin soup was banned by the Chinese government from being served at state banquets. This marked a clear sign that shark-fin soup had lost status, and another major market had closed off. The decline in demand became visible soon afterwards. WildAid conducted a survey online in 2013, which included 1,568 people from Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Chengdu. Some 85 per cent of respondents said they had stopped eating shark-fin soup in the previous three years. Of those who stopped eating it, about two-thirds cited awareness campaigns as one factor in their decision.Research published in Marine Policy similarly noted that consumer-awareness campaigns featuring celebrities such as Yao Ming and Jackie Chan had helped raise awareness, although it stressed that it was difficult to separate their effect from other factors behind the decline in consumption. More than 80 per cent of respondents in Beijing and Shanghai had seen Yao’s advertisements, showing the campaign’s reach.What happened to sharks?This change in consumption in China was a major development, but it did not address the global issue of sharks. Sharks are still at risk of overfishing, bycatch, and the international trade of their fins and meat. According to WildAid, fins from millions of sharks continue to appear on the global market each year, while more than a third of shark species are endangered. However, the example of China offers a more complex lesson.Nevertheless, Yao Ming provided something hard to engineer: a familiar face that challenged the social status of shark-fin soup. Starting in 2006, when Yao Ming publicly rejected the dish, the campaign became part of a broader shift in how shark-fin soup was perceived.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Beijing tightens drone crackdown, bans possession and storage across city from November 15
articles.summary: China News: Beijing will ban residents and businesses from possessing or storing drones and key drone components within the city from November 15, authorities sai.
articles.body: Beijing will ban residents and businesses from possessing or storing drones and key drone components within the city from November 15, authorities said, tightening restrictions on the devices after a series of security measures introduced earlier this year.The revised rules, approved this month and released on Sunday, will allow authorities to confiscate drones from those who violate the ban and impose fines on individuals and companies. Existing owners will be offered subsidies to sell or scrap their drones before the new rules take effect.The move marks the latest step in Beijing's tightening regulation of drones. The city had already banned unauthorised drone flights and designated its entire administrative area as restricted airspace on security grounds.Under rules approved in March and effective from May 1, existing drone owners were required to register their devices using their real names and identities. They were initially allowed to keep their registered drones, subject to strict requirements.The latest rules go further by banning possession and storage altogether within Beijing's city limits.According to the state-owned newspaper Beijing Daily, existing drone owners can sell their devices at designated buyback locations and receive a subsidy. They can also scrap and recycle the drones with a smaller subsidy, or move them outside Beijing before November 15.The tightening comes after a fatal accident in late June, when a small aircraft crashed into a skyscraper in Beijing. The crash killed the pilot and injured 13 people.Drones can still be flown outdoors in other parts of China, although users must register them under their real names. Beijing, the Chinese capital, has often imposed stricter security rules than other parts of the country.Bringing drones into Beijing from outside the city, including by tourists, is already prohibited.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Gautam Budh Nagar district magistrate Medha Roopam moved Supreme Court days after she was reprimanded over the detention of a student protester under the National Security Act.This comes after Allahabad high court quashed the NSA against Akriti Chaudhary - a 25-year-old student - who was taken into custody in connection with Noida worker's protest in April.The court found that the detention was based on a story "concocted" by the state and directed her immediate release if her arrest was not warranted in any other case.It also directed that a compensation amount of Rs 5 lakh be deducted from Medha Roopam's salary. articles.title: In 2000, Martha Stewart bought a 152-acre New York farmhouse; 26 years later, the horse farm has 100+ chickens and 11 pheasants after she added 13 chickens and a silver pheasant
articles.summary: US News: When Martha Stewart purchased a 152-acre farmhouse in Katonah, New York, in 2000, the property was more than a country retreat. It became a working fa.
articles.body: When Martha Stewart purchased a 152-acre farmhouse in Katonah, New York, in 2000, the property was more than a country retreat. It became a working farm, creative laboratory and carefully managed home for an ever-growing collection of animals. Over the next 26 years, the former farmhouse evolved into Bedford Farm, also known as Cantitoe Corners, with horses, gardens, historic and modern buildings, and a remarkable variety of poultry. Stewart has said she keeps more than 100 chickens of different breeds. In recent years, she added 13 new birds, including Araucanas, Silkies, Sultans, Polish chickens, Buff Orpingtons and Rhode Island Reds. She later welcomed a young male silver pheasant, bringing the farm’s pheasant population to 11. Her own website offers a close look at how the property became a living expression of her love of animals, gardening and country life.From farmhouse to farmsteadStewart bought the 1925 farmhouse in 2000, after years of transforming other properties into distinctive homes. Unlike a simple weekend estate, the 152-acre Katonah property offered enough land for a working horse farm and a broad range of agricultural activities.The house and grounds became known as Bedford Farm or Cantitoe Corners. Stewart’s approach was not to erase the property’s history, but to combine old and new. Historic buildings sit alongside modern structures, while gardens, paddocks and animal enclosures are organised across the land.The farm has become one of the places most closely associated with Stewart’s public image. It reflects her interest in horticulture, architecture, food and animal care. The property also provides the setting for many of her photographs and stories, allowing followers to see not only finished gardens and beautiful birds but also the daily work required to maintain them.A large farm is never static. Plants grow, buildings need repair and animals arrive, mature and sometimes leave. Stewart’s additions to the poultry population show how the property continues to evolve more than two decades after she bought it.A flock with personalityStewart’s interest in chickens extends beyond their usefulness. She has described raising chickens and other fowl as rewarding because of their beauty and companionship. Her flock includes many breeds, each with different colours, feather patterns, body shapes and temperaments.The diversity can be seen in the birds she selected from the Northeastern Poultry Congress in Springfield, Massachusetts. The annual event features thousands of birds, including chickens, ducks, turkeys, pigeons, geese and other fowl. For Stewart, it is a place to admire unusual breeds and meet breeders with specialised knowledge.Her flock includes Araucanas, Silkies, Sultans, Crested Polish chickens, Buff Orpingtons and Rhode Island Reds. These breeds look and behave differently. Araucana hens are known for laying eggs with pale blue shells, while Polish chickens are recognised for their dramatic crests.The birds’ differences are part of their appeal. Some have elaborate plumage, others are valued for their egg production and some are kept simply because their appearance adds character to the farm. Together, they create a living collection that changes as new chicks hatch and young birds mature.Thirteen new arrivalsOne recent expansion brought 13 new chickens to the farm. The birds came from the poultry show and represented several breeds that added new colours and features to the existing flock.When the chickens arrived, Stewart placed them in an enclosure reserved for new birds. This separation gave them time to settle into the farm and helped lessen risks that can develop when unfamiliar birds are introduced directly into an established flock. They were expected to join the other chickens later. The arrival process is representative of the practical side of keeping poultry. Adding beautiful birds to a farm requires more than selecting breeds. New animals need a safe enclosure, suitable food and water, protection from predators and time to settle into their surroundings. Each bird also needs observation. Farm caretakers need to look for signs of illness, stress or difficulty adapting.When the birds are eventually mixed with the established flock, their interactions must be monitored to ensure that the group remains healthy and stable.For Stewart, the process also creates an opportunity to introduce followers to poultry care. The birds are visually appealing, but their wellbeing depends on routine, planning and attention.The silver pheasant arrivesAfter welcoming the chickens, Stewart expanded her collection of ornamental birds with a young male silver pheasant. The arrival brought her total number of pheasants to 11. Most of the farm’s pheasants are golden pheasants, including birds with different colour variations. The new silver pheasant stood out for its long tail and silvery white and grey feathers marked with darker patterns. As the bird matures, its plumage is expected to change, with the crest and central feathers becoming more pronounced. At first, the young bird needed some time to get settled into its new environment. Stewart saw that it was starting to go out and enjoy the company of its new friends. This gradual introduction allowed the pheasant to get acclimated to its environment without being overwhelmed. Silver pheasants are ground dwelling birds, although they can perch when looking for safety or avoiding predators. Their calm and docile nature can make them appealing additions to a carefully managed private farm. Their striking appearance also makes them natural subjects for photography.Stewart’s pheasant collection includes different colour varieties, each requiring attention to its environment. Some golden pheasants need shade to help preserve the brightness of their feathers, particularly when direct sunlight can affect their colouring.Why the birds matter to the farmThe chickens and pheasants are not merely decorative features. They contribute to the farm's atmosphere and rhythm. Their care brings about routines of feeding, cleaning, observation and protection. Their presence also links the property to older country ways of living, when farms typically had a mix of livestock and poultry. For Stewart, the birds fit in naturally with her gardens and culinary interests. Chickens supply eggs, and their behavior and look bring life to the landscape.They give color and movement, often perching among trees, paths and planted areas. The farm is also a place of education. Stewart shows features of different breeds in photographs and articles and explains how the birds are housed.Her posts encourage people to look at poultry as more than a uniform category of farm animal.At a time when many people encounter animals mainly through screens or supermarkets, the farm offers a more detailed picture of their care. It shows that eggs, feathers and ornamental beauty all depend on living animals with specific needs.A carefully managed collectionKeeping more than 100 chickens alongside 11 pheasants requires organisation.Birds need suitable shelters, secure fencing, clean water and protection from predators. Different species and breeds may also have different nutritional or environmental requirements.The farm’s size helps create space for separate enclosures and specialised areas. New arrivals can be quarantined or observed before joining established groups. Birds that need shade can be placed in suitable areas, while those that prefer higher perches can be given structures that allow them to roost safely.The size of the property also allows Stewart to keep the farm from feeling like a crowded collection. The animals can move through designed spaces while remaining under supervision. That balance between freedom and protection is an important part of responsible private animal care.The birds’ changing appearance adds another element of interest. Young pheasants do not always look like adults, and some chicken breeds develop their distinctive feathers as they mature. Watching those changes gives the farm a sense of continuity and anticipation.A home shaped by living thingsStewart’s New York property is often discussed through its gardens, architecture and interiors, but the animals reveal another side of the estate. A farm is shaped by living systems. Seasons influence planting, weather affects the birds and daily care determines how the animals thrive.The addition of 13 chickens and a silver pheasant shows that Cantitoe Corners is not a finished display. It remains a place of activity and change. New birds alter the routines of the farm, create fresh stories and add to the variety of life already present.That quality distinguishes the property from a conventional luxury estate. Its value lies not only in its size or design but in the way the land is used. Gardens produce flowers and food, buildings support farm work, and animals become part of the household’s daily experience. After 26 years, the farmhouse has become a carefully cultivated ecosystem, reflecting Stewart’s belief that beauty can be found in both formal design and ordinary care.More than a celebrity hobbyStewart’s poultry collection may attract attention because of her fame, but the interest in the birds also reflects a wider revival of backyard poultry and rare breed conservation. People increasingly want to understand where food comes from, keep small flocks or preserve heritage breeds that are less common in commercial agriculture.Rare and ornamental breeds can carry historical and genetic value. Maintaining them helps preserve traits that might otherwise disappear.Their colours, feather patterns, egg characteristics and behaviours form part of agricultural heritage.Stewart’s public documentation gives these breeds visibility. A photograph of a crested Polish chicken or a silver pheasant can inspire someone to learn more about poultry care, attend a local show or support a responsible breeder.The message is not that everyone needs a 152-acre farm. It is that keeping animals well requires knowledge, commitment and respect for their needs.Stewart’s property provides a large scale example of how those principles can shape country life.A farm that keeps growingWhen Stewart bought the farmhouse in 2000, she acquired the space to create a long term rural home. Since then, Bedford Farm has grown into a horse farm and a sanctuary for gardens, buildings and animals.The flock of more than 100 chickens and the 11 pheasants are part of that continuing story. The arrival of 13 chickens added new breeds and personalities, while the silver pheasant introduced another distinctive bird to the grounds.Each addition brings colour, companionship and another reason to pay attention to the everyday life of the farm.What began as a property purchase became a decades long project of cultivation. Stewart shaped the land, but the land also shaped her routines and interests. Today, the farmhouse is defined not only by its rooms or acreage but by the gardens that grow, the horses that move through the fields and the birds that fill the enclosures with sound and colour.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
